documents.unit: Academic Senate, Council on Educational Policy
documents.title: Guidelines for Course Syllabi (Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy section)
documents.summary: Academic Senate syllabus guidelines require every syllabus to carry a generative AI policy, state there is no campus policy, and leave content to the instructor. Gives tips on writing the policy: course or assignment level, rationale, enforcement, and ZotGPT.
documents.stance_why: It says 'All course syllabi must include a policy' but 'There is no general campus policy ... and the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor', so it sets no stance and hands the decision to instructors.

units.why: Syllabus rule: 'All course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI', so it requires every instructor to state AI expectations in the syllabus (P09), binding instructors before the course.
units.anchor: All course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI

units.why: States there is no campus-wide rule and 'the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor', which hands the stance to each instructor (P04); it informs rather than binds.
units.anchor: the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor
units.policy: There is no general campus policy on student use of generative AI, and the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor.

units.why: 'Your policy should provide guidance at the course level and/or the assignment level' lets the rule be set per course or per assignment, so P04 rather than P05 (no named tiers).
units.anchor: Your policy should provide guidance at the course level and/or the assignment level.

units.why: Tells instructors to weigh each task and 'whether using generative AI might facilitate or impede student learning', tying the AI decision to learning aims (P83); it fits partly because it names tasks, not formal objectives.
units.anchor: whether using generative AI might facilitate or impede student learning in completing the tasks
units.policy: Instructors consider the tasks in the course and in each assignment and whether using generative AI might facilitate or impede student learning in completing them.
units.fit_note: Framed as a task-by-task judgment about helping or impeding learning rather than alignment to stated learning objectives.

units.why: Advises instructors to keep current on AI tools since 'apps and third-party platforms often update their features', which is staying informed (P102) so the policy can be updated.
units.anchor: it is important to have the most up-to-date understanding of those capabilities before course delivery
units.policy: Instructors should have the most up-to-date understanding of AI tool capabilities before course delivery, in case the policy needs to be updated.

units.why: 'Your syllabus should explain how and why using generative AI is or is not acceptable', telling instructors to give students the reasons for the rule (P66), not only list it.
units.anchor: explain how and why using generative AI is or is not acceptable

units.why: Notes AI may be 'a helpful learning tool' in some places and 'strictly forbidden' in others within one course, endorsing per-activity rules (P04) and differentiating among cases.
units.anchor: AI is a helpful learning tool and others where it is strictly forbidden
units.policy: Within a course there may be cases where AI is a helpful learning tool and others where it is strictly forbidden.

units.why: 'encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as ZotGPT' where AI is allowed: points to university-provided tools institution-wide, so P92 not P17 (not one course's tool).
units.anchor: encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as
units.policy: If a course policy allows AI, instructors encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as ZotGPT and other tools built by UCI, when possible.

units.why: Tells instructors to 'explain what aspects of learning the policy is intended to safeguard', giving students the rationale; closest is P66 (explain the rules), partly because it asks for the learning being protected.
units.anchor: explain what aspects of learning the policy is intended to safeguard
units.policy: To bolster student understanding and adherence, instructors explain what aspects of learning the policy is intended to safeguard.
units.fit_note: Specifically asks the instructor to name the aspects of learning the rule protects.

units.why: Instructors should 'explain what constitutes a violation of academic integrity' in the AI policy: defines misuse for students; no type is about telling students what counts as a violation, and P66 is stretched here, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: explain what constitutes a violation of academic integrity
units.policy: Instructors explain to students what constitutes a violation of academic integrity under the AI policy.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must tell students what counts as an AI-related academic-integrity violation.

units.why: 'Describe how the policy will be enforced in the course' asks each instructor to state enforcement up front; no type covers announcing the enforcement approach, so UNCOVERED (P37 requires specific penalties, which this does not).
units.anchor: Describe how the policy will be enforced in the course.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors state in the syllabus how the AI policy will be enforced, without specifying penalties.

documents.unit: Division of Teaching Excellence and Innovation (Office of the Vice Provost for Teaching and Learning)
documents.title: Generative AI: Is my AI policy - and the rationale - clear on the syllabus?
documents.summary: Teaching center page restating the Senate and Graduate Council requirements for an AI policy in every syllabus. Explains the absence of a campus policy as intentional and asks instructors for clear, course-specific rules.
documents.stance_why: It states 'There is no single campuswide policy' and 'the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor', so it delegates.

units.why: Says the Senate 'now requires that all undergraduate course syllabi include a clear statement addressing the use of generative AI tools', a syllabus-statement mandate (P09) addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: all undergraduate course syllabi include a clear statement addressing the use of generative AI tools

units.why: Graduate Council rule: 'All graduate course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI'; same type as the undergraduate rule but a separate body and population, so coded separately (P09).
units.anchor: All graduate course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI

units.why: 'There is no single campuswide policy ... the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor' places the decision on instructors (P04).
units.anchor: the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor
units.policy: There is no single campuswide policy governing student use of generative AI; the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor.

units.why: 'Graduate programs are also expected to include this requirement ... in their program handbooks' asks programs (admin) to repeat the AI-policy requirement; P09 fits as a statement requirement, here at the program level.
units.anchor: Graduate programs are also expected to include this requirement
units.policy: Graduate programs are expected to include the requirement for an AI policy, along with appropriate language, in their program handbooks.
units.fit_note: Applies to graduate program handbooks, not syllabi.

units.why: Explains that 'the absence of a single campuswide policy is intentional' because AI's role varies by discipline and level: the reason for delegating (P04), informs.
units.anchor: the absence of a single campuswide policy is intentional

units.why: 'In some contexts, AI tools may support exploration, drafting, or problem-solving' names benefits of AI in teaching without making a rule (P87 over P02, since nothing is allowed by default).
units.anchor: AI tools may support exploration, drafting, or problem-solving

units.why: 'their use may be limited or prohibited to preserve specific learning outcomes' ties limits to learning outcomes, matching P83 (decisions follow learning objectives).
units.anchor: limited or prohibited to preserve specific learning outcomes or forms of assessment

units.why: 'instructors are best positioned to define appropriate use within their own courses' justifies instructor-set rules (P04).
units.anchor: instructors are best positioned to define appropriate use within their own courses

units.why: 'Develop a clear, course-specific policy' is expected of all instructors, and a course-specific policy means each course sets its own rule (P04); expectation language, so should.
units.anchor: Develop a clear, course-specific policy on student use of generative AI

units.why: 'Communicate that policy explicitly in the course syllabus' is the expectation to state the AI policy in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: Communicate that policy explicitly in the course syllabus

units.why: 'Ensure that expectations are transparent and consistently applied' is about clarity and consistent application of the AI rules; closest P09 (state expectations) but consistency of application goes beyond it.
units.anchor: Ensure that expectations are transparent and consistently applied
units.fit_note: Also asks that the expectations be consistently applied, not only stated.

units.why: 'Clear guidance helps students understand not only what is permitted, but why' states that explaining the reason behind rules is valuable (P66).
units.anchor: Clear guidance helps students understand not only what is permitted, but why.

units.why: 'this is an evolving space' acknowledges the area is changing, nearest P54 (policy is provisional), but it does not say the policy will be revisited.
units.anchor: We recognize that this is an evolving space
units.policy: We recognize that this is an evolving space.
units.fit_note: Acknowledges change but does not commit to a review or revision.

units.why: Encourages instructors to 'align your course policies with your learning goals and values', so AI rules follow learning goals (P83).
units.anchor: align your course policies with your learning goals and values as educators

documents.unit: Division of Teaching Excellence and Innovation
documents.title: Syllabus Policies Governing Student Use of AI (five example statements)
tiers: AI used only for editing and grammar check
AI: use but cite and explain
AI encouraged with guardrails and caveats
documents.summary: Five sample syllabus statements from prohibition to encouragement, with the curator's advice to adapt per assignment and repeat expectations. Each sample sets rules a given instructor could adopt.
documents.stance_why: It offers examples that 'span the gamut from AI use prohibited to AI use encouraged/facilitated' to be 'adapted', setting no stance itself, so it delegates and lists five templates as tiers.

units.why: Intro says the examples 'span the gamut from AI use prohibited to AI use encouraged/facilitated', i.e. a menu of levels of AI use (P05), informing instructors.
units.anchor: span the gamut from AI use prohibited to AI use encouraged/facilitated

units.why: 'you are free to use as is or adapt' offers sample verbiage that instructors choose from, so each instructor sets the rule (P04); the text is optional help, hence may.
units.anchor: five examples of syllabi verbiage that you are free to use as is or adapt

units.why: 'can and should be adapted for specific assignments based on your pedagogical rationale' tells instructors to tune AI rules per assignment (P04).
units.anchor: can and should be adapted for specific assignments based on your pedagogical rationale

units.why: 'Practice planned redundancy by reminding students of your individual assignment policies' in class, assignment instructions, rubrics and announcements: repeated communication of expectations (P09 nearest, but it asks for reminders, not just a statement).
units.anchor: reminding students of your individual assignment policies
units.policy: Instructors practice planned redundancy by reminding students of their individual assignment policies in class time, assignment instructions, assignment rubrics or Canvas announcements.
units.fit_note: Asks for repeated reminders through several channels beyond the syllabus statement.

units.why: Recommends a primer by the Mollicks 'for using AI in your classroom', offering faculty learning resources (P63).
units.anchor: One of the better primers for using AI in your classroom

units.why: Example 1 reason: 'it is critical for you to develop core research and writing skills first before adding AI', i.e. fundamentals before AI (P42 over P41, because the point is order and foundations).
units.anchor: develop core research and writing skills first before adding AI and other tools

units.why: 'The danger in letting an AI platform undertake your synthesis and writing is that you will not develop these important skills': AI limits justified by skill-building (P41).
units.anchor: platform undertake your synthesis and writing is that you will not develop these important skills

units.why: 'AI bots are famous for making things up' warns outputs can be wrong (P31).
units.anchor: AI bots are famous for making things up.

units.why: 'the course policy is to avoid using AI at all for your assignments' is a ban on AI for assignments, the default prohibition (P01).
units.anchor: the course policy is to avoid using AI at all for your assignments

units.why: Example 2: 'complete your work without using AI-generated sources to augment, think through, or write your assignments' bans AI unless excepted, so a default prohibition (P01) with a narrow exception below.
units.anchor: complete your work without using AI-generated sources to augment, think through, or write your assignments

units.why: The exception: 'welcome to use AI tools for pre-submission editing (spell-check and grammar-check)' allows narrow editing uses (P91; P100 is for routine features under any rule, but here the allowance is the point).
units.anchor: you are welcome to use AI tools for pre-submission editing (spell-check and grammar-check)

units.why: 'as long as you do not use them for thinking or drafting' limits the editing exception: AI may not do the thinking or drafting (P19).
units.anchor: as long as you do not use them for thinking or drafting
units.fit_note: Bans thinking and drafting with AI rather than generating the submitted text specifically.

units.why: 'I will ask you to meet with me to discuss your thinking and writing process' is a conversation with the student before escalating (P57).
units.anchor: I will ask you to meet with me to discuss your thinking and writing process

units.why: 'more likely than not' sets a standard of proof for finding the student did not do the work, an evidence standard (P69).
units.anchor: more likely than not that you did not personally complete an assignment

units.why: 'I may report a violation to the campus Office of Academic Integrity & Student Conduct' sends suspected unauthorized AI use to the integrity process (P36).
units.anchor: I may report a violation to the campus Office of Academic Integrity & Student Conduct

units.why: Example 3: 'you are welcome to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) models' is a default permission with conditions (P02).
units.anchor: you are welcome to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) models with acknowledgment

units.why: 'its contribution must be cited and discussed' requires disclosure of any AI use with the submission (P24).
units.anchor: its contribution must be cited and discussed

units.why: 'all large language models have a tendency to make up facts and citations and perpetuate biases' warns outputs can be wrong or biased (P31).
units.anchor: large language models have a tendency to make up facts and citations and perpetuate biases

units.why: 'Image generation models can occasionally come up with offensive images' names a harm of AI (P53).
units.anchor: Image generation models can occasionally come up with offensive images.

units.why: 'You will be responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content you submit' makes the student responsible for submitted work (P29).
units.anchor: You will be responsible for any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or otherwise unethical content you submit

units.why: 'What AI tool did you use?' with 'What was your prompt?' lists the tool and prompt the citation must give, which is P25.
units.anchor: What AI tool did you use?
units.policy: The citation states which AI tool was used and what the prompt was.

units.why: 'What did you learn?' joins questions about revision and follow-ups that the discussion must answer: a reflection on AI use (P26).
units.anchor: What did you learn?
units.policy: The discussion of the AI contribution answers whether the output was revised, whether follow-up questions were asked, and what was learned.

units.why: Example 4: 'I encourage students to use ZotGPT' promotes the university's tool for listed tasks, institution-wide and not a course-built bot, so P92.
units.anchor: I encourage students to use ZotGPT for the following types of tasks

units.why: 'Outlining content' is a listed encouraged task, organizing writing (P91).
units.anchor: Outlining content
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use ZotGPT for outlining content.

units.why: 'Providing background knowledge' lets students use ZotGPT like a tutor or search engine for concepts (P12).
units.anchor: Providing background knowledge
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use ZotGPT for providing background knowledge.

units.why: 'ZotGPT is often wrong—Wikipedia is a better resource' warns outputs are unreliable (P31).
units.anchor: ZotGPT is often wrong—Wikipedia is a better resource for this right now

units.why: 'Checking grammar and syntax' is an encouraged use of ZotGPT for editing own writing (P91).
units.anchor: Checking grammar and syntax
units.policy: Students are encouraged to use ZotGPT for checking grammar and syntax.

units.why: 'you MUST do the following: Cite ZotGPT' requires citing the tool with the submission (P24).
units.anchor: Cite ZotGPT
units.policy: If students use ZotGPT, they must cite ZotGPT.

units.why: 'Write a brief paragraph at the end of your work explaining how and why you used ZotGPT' is a required reflection on AI use (P26).
units.anchor: brief paragraph at the end of your work explaining how and why you used ZotGPT

units.why: 'Include the prompts you used' requires giving the prompts (P25).
units.anchor: Include the prompts you used

units.why: 'Who is the author of this work? Then explain your answer.' makes students reason about authorship, nearest P29 (own what you submit) but it is a required explanation.
units.anchor: answer this question: Who is the author of this work?
units.policy: Students answer the question 'Who is the author of this work?' and explain their answer.
units.fit_note: Authorship is raised as a required question and explanation, not as a plain ownership rule.

units.why: 'I reserve the right ... to require you to revise and resubmit' states a consequence for inappropriate use; nearest P37 (concrete penalties), but it is a remedial resubmission not a grade penalty.
units.anchor: require you to revise and resubmit all or parts of the assignment
units.fit_note: The consequence is revise-and-resubmit, not a grade penalty.

units.why: 'you have not included the required citation and reflection' makes missing disclosure the trigger for action, so non-disclosure is the problem (P28).
units.anchor: you have not included the required citation and reflection
units.fit_note: Non-disclosure triggers a meeting rather than a stated violation.

units.why: 'This conversation will include knowledge checks for course content' checks understanding by questioning the student (P34).
units.anchor: This conversation will include knowledge checks for course content.

units.why: Example 5: 'I expect you to use AI in this class' expects use, so default encouragement (P02).
units.anchor: I expect you to use AI in this class.

units.why: 'some assignments will require it' builds AI into coursework (P79).
units.anchor: some assignments will require it

units.why: 'Learning to use AI is an emerging skill, and I will provide basic tutorials' frames AI use as a skill the course teaches (P44).
units.anchor: Learning to use AI is an emerging skill, and I will provide basic tutorials

units.why: 'AI is vulnerable to discrimination because it can ... perpetuate existing biases' names bias as a concern (P53).
units.anchor: AI is vulnerable to discrimination because it can inadvertently (or intentionally) perpetuate existing biases

units.why: 'AI can be a valuable tool for augmenting human decision-making and critical thinking, but it is not a replacement' says AI must not replace the student's thinking (P32).
units.anchor: AI can be a valuable tool for augmenting human decision-making and critical thinking

units.why: 'unlike most tools you need to acknowledge using it' requires acknowledging AI use (P24).
units.anchor: unlike most tools you need to acknowledge using it

units.why: 'explain how/what you used at the end of assignments' requires a statement of what AI was used for (P24).
units.anchor: explain how/what you used at the end of assignments

units.why: 'My recommendation is to screen shot and save everything' advises keeping prompts and answers, a transcript practice (P26); recommended, not required.
units.anchor: My recommendation is to screen shot and save everything

units.why: 'Cite everything' with 'basic attribution rules still apply' requires citing all AI-produced material (P24).
units.anchor: Cite everything

units.why: 'otherwise you are likely violating academic integrity policies' makes uncited AI use a violation, i.e. non-disclosure as the violation (P28).
units.anchor: otherwise you are likely violating academic integrity policies

units.why: 'If you provide minimum effort prompts, you will get low quality results' advises on prompt quality (P93).
units.anchor: You will need to refine your prompts to get better outcomes.

units.why: 'Don't trust anything the system says. Assume it is wrong' tells students to verify output (P31).
units.anchor: Assume it is wrong, unless you already know the answer and can verify

units.why: 'Use your best judgment to determine if/where/when to use these tools' leaves each student to decide; no type covers student self-judgment, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Use your best judgment to determine if/where/when to use these tools.
units.uncovered_note: Within a permissive policy, students decide for themselves if, where and when to use AI.

notes: Only the three included university-layer documents were coded; the ICS 33 and ICS H32 course documents were deferred. In the statements document, example statements are sample language an instructor may adopt, coded as policies they state. Several UNCOVERED notes concern instructors telling students what counts as a violation and how the policy will be enforced.
